title: manifesting, honestly
hookLine: vision boards and billions of views: what's psychology, what's belief, and where it came from
carry: picture the wish, then the wall

cards: Vision boards. Scripting in a journal. Saying it like it's already yours.
Manifesting has billions of views online, and lately a lot of people say it's started to feel a little fake. That's a fair instinct. It isn't ancient, and it isn't a secret.
The idea grew up in America about a hundred and fifty years ago. Some of it holds up surprisingly well. Some of it doesn't.

teach.b: In the 1800s, an American movement called New Thought taught that the mind shapes health and fortune: change the thought, change the life. Its writers are mostly forgotten now, but their phrases aren't.
In 2006 a book called The Secret gathered their ideas under one name, the law of attraction, and sold tens of millions of copies. Now, honestly.

There's no good evidence that a thought, on its own, pulls a thing toward you. And the strong version has a cruel flip side: if things go wrong, you must have thought wrong. Nothing backs that, and it isn't kind.
First, naming what you want changes what you notice. Decide you want a new job, and openings start jumping out at you. Second, the psychologist Gabriele Oettingen found something surprising.
People who only daydream about the dream tend to put in less effort, and often get less of it.
What works better is to picture the wish, then picture what's in the way, and make a plan: when this happens, I'll do that. So keep the vision board, if you love it.
Just give it a second column: the wall, and the way over it.

how: People who manifest often write or picture a goal every day, on a vision board or in a journal; some coaches and therapists teach mental contrasting instead, pairing the wish with its obstacle and an if-then plan.

games.q: where it came from, what holds up — tap the pairs.

s: manifesting is an ancient spiritual secret
it grew out of New Thought, an American movement of the 1800s.
only daydreaming about a goal can leave people trying less
in Oettingen's studies, pure positive fantasy often came with less effort.
research shows a thought, by itself, pulls an outcome toward you
there's no good evidence for that. naming a goal does change what you notice.

games.q: you want to run a half marathon. which plan does Oettingen's research favor?
o: picture crossing the finish line every night.
picture the finish, then the rainy mornings, and plan for them.
tell everyone, so you have to do it.
games.why: the wish, then the obstacle, then an if-then plan. she calls it mental contrasting.

games.q: put Oettingen's four steps in order.

practice: Three breaths with the bell. On the first, picture one thing you want this year, as clearly as you can. On the second, picture the main thing in the way: a habit, a fear, a full calendar.
On the third, make one small plan: when that happens, I'll…

wordCard.voice: Manifesting. An American idea from the 1800s with a new name. Keep the wish; add the wall. Fifth word.

carryVoice: Your line: picture the wish, then the wall. The second half is the part the research backs. Day five, done.
